response.title: Is it better to run extension cords from a power station to the fridge and furnace or pay for a hookup at the panel?
response.answer:
If you're planning to use a portable power station for backup power during outages, I'd lean toward paying for a proper panel hookup, especially since you want to power both your refrigerator and furnace.

However, the best choice depends on how frequently you lose power, your power station's capacity, and how much the installation costs.

Comparing the two options
	

Extension cords

	

Panel hookup




Upfront cost

~$500–$2,000+




Refrigerator

	

Easy

Gas furnace

	

Often difficult

	

Easy with correct setup




Setup during outage

	

Run cords manually

	

Switch circuits over




Safety

	

Safe if properly sized and used

	

Safer and cleaner when professionally installed




Convenience

	

Low

	

High




Flexibility

	

Can move power station around

	

Primarily tied to house

Costs are rough U.S. estimates; installation prices vary considerably by panel and location.

Why the furnace changes the equation

Your refrigerator is relatively straightforward. Most refrigerators plug into a standard 120V outlet, so a properly rated extension cord can work.

Your furnace is different.

Most gas furnaces are hardwired into your home's electrical system. Even though they burn natural gas for heat, they still need electricity for the blower, control board, and ignition.

You have three practical options:

Extension cords: If your furnace has an approved plug-and-receptacle connection, you may be able to power it directly. A hardwired furnace needs an appropriate, code-compliant connection rather than an improvised cord.

Furnace transfer switch: An electrician can install a dedicated transfer arrangement for the furnace. This may be cheaper than connecting the whole panel.

Panel transfer switch or interlock: Allows your power station to supply selected home circuits through existing wiring, subject to compatibility and electrical-code requirements.

Never backfeed your house through an ordinary outlet or use a double-male extension cord.

What I'd recommend
Shop

Occasional outages (once or twice a year)

Use an extension cord for the refrigerator and consider a dedicated furnace transfer connection. This keeps installation costs down.

Shop

Frequent or prolonged outages

A professionally installed panel connection is worth considering. It lets you power the fridge, furnace, lights, and other selected circuits without cords throughout the house.

One important consideration: not every power station supports a panel connection. Some have only 120V outputs, some cannot provide sufficient starting power, and furnace controls can be sensitive to grounding and neutral configurations. A licensed electrician should verify compatibility and install a listed transfer device or approved interlock that prevents utility backfeed.

Three questions that would help me make a specific recommendation
Which power station do you have?
What type of furnace?
Natural gas
Propane
Electric / heat pump
How often do you lose power?
Rarely, perhaps 1–2 times a year
Several times a year
Outages sometimes last multiple days
Get my hookup recommendation

With those details, I can help determine whether a $200–$500-ish dedicated furnace connection might be sufficient or whether a full panel hookup is worth the additional expense.
